claim: Male rats were used in all experiments, aged 6-12 months with weight maintained between 400 and 500 g.
source: All experiments were done in male Long Evans rats 6–12 months of age (with weight kept between 400 and 500 g).
evidence: Direct statement in the Methods section describing the experimental subjects.

claim: Animals were kept at 85% of their initial body weight before food restriction.
source: Animals were kept at 85% of their initial body weight before food restriction and maintained on a 12 hr light/12 hr dark schedule.
evidence: Direct statement in the Methods section describing animal maintenance procedures.

claim: A total of 7 animals were implanted with tetrode drives for neural activity collection during the task.
source: A total of 7 animals were implanted with tetrode drives for collection of neural activity during the task (4 animals targeting the ACC and 3 animals targeting the SMC).
evidence: Direct statement in the Methods section describing the number of animals used.

claim: Four animals were implanted targeting the ACC and three animals targeting the SMC.
source: A total of 7 animals were implanted with tetrode drives for collection of neural activity during the task (4 animals targeting the ACC and 3 animals targeting the SMC).
evidence: Direct statement in the Methods section describing the distribution of recording targets.

claim: The behavioral apparatus consisted of a box with 23 cm high plastic walls and stainless-steel floors.
source: All behavior was confined to a box with 23 cm high plastic walls and stainless-steel floors (Island Motion Corp).
evidence: Direct statement in the Methods section describing the behavioral apparatus.

claim: The floor of the behavioral box was 25 cm by 34 cm.
source: The floor of the box was 25 cm by 34 cm, and the nose ports were all arranged on one of the 25 cm walls.
evidence: Direct statement in the Methods section describing the apparatus dimensions.

claim: Nose port entries were detected with an infrared beam-break detector consisting of an IR LED and photodiode pair.
source: Nose port entries were detected with an infrared beam-break detector (IR LED and photodiode pair).
evidence: Direct statement in the Methods section describing the detection method.

claim: Liquid rewards consisted of 0.1 ml drops of 10% sucrose mixed with black cherry Kool-Aid.
source: The side ports also delivered liquid rewards (0.1 ml drops of 10% sucrose mixed with black cherry Kool-Aid) with the help of a motorized syringe pump (Harvard Apparatus PHD 2000).
evidence: Direct statement in the Methods section describing the reward composition.

claim: Expert animals flexibly and reliably discovered and exploited the locally-relevant latent target within tens of trials following block transitions.
source: Under these conditions, expert animals flexibly and reliably discovered and exploited the locally-relevant latent target: within tens of trials following block transitions, the animals' choices typically became dominated by the new target sequence, even in the presence of substantial (up to 30%) sporadic omission of reward for the properly executed target sequence (Figures 1b–c–2b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in figures and described in the text.

claim: Animals' choices became dominated by the new target sequence even with up to 30% sporadic omission of reward.
source: Under these conditions, expert animals flexibly and reliably discovered and exploited the locally-relevant latent target: within tens of trials following block transitions, the animals' choices typically became dominated by the new target sequence, even in the presence of substantial (up to 30%) sporadic omission of reward for the properly executed target sequence (Figures 1b–c–2b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing robust performance despite reward omission.

claim: A simple linear classifier could reliably distinguish ACC activity between 'LLR' and 'RRL' sequences with median cross-validated classification error of 0.0 (IQR 0.006).
source: A simple linear classifier could reliably distinguish ACC activity between 'LLR' and 'RRL' sequences – the two main target sequences in our dataset – when provided with firing rates of all active cells in 500 ms windows centered on side port entries for the three steps in each sequence (Figure 1—figure supplement 3 median cross-validated classification error 0.0, IQR 0.006, Methods).
evidence: Quantitative results from linear classification analysis reported with specific error values.

claim: Robust classification of sequences was achieved when the decoding window was anchored on the initiation (center) port entry prior to when the overt choice was made.
source: Robust classification was also achieved when the decoding window for each of the three sequence steps was instead anchored on the initiation (center) port entry common to all trials, prior to when the overt choice on that trial was made by the animal (Figure 1d, median cross-validated classification error 0.0, IQR 0.007, Methods).
evidence: Quantitative results from classification analysis with center port-centered windows.

claim: There is strong difference in the encoding of individual steps composing the sequences ('L' vs 'R') in ACC.
source: Nevertheless, any interpretation of the decodability of the full 'LLR' vs 'RRL' ACC representations is confounded by a strong difference in the encoding of the individual steps composing the sequences ('L' vs 'R'; Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, median cross-validated classification error 0.008, IQR 0.016 and 0.009, 0.0017 for side port-centered and center port-centered decoding windows respectively).
evidence: Quantitative results from classification analysis showing encoding differences.

claim: The encoding of the same action 'R' differs between 'LLR' and 'RRL' sequences, with median cross-validated error of 0.10 (IQR 0.14) for side port-centered windows.
source: We indeed found that even controlling for the specific action in this manner, the corresponding neural activity could be used to accurately decode whether that action was embedded in 'LLR' versus 'RRL' sequences (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 3; median cross-validated error 0.10, IQR 0.14 and 0.08, 0.13 for side port-centered and center-port centered decoding windows, respectively).
evidence: Quantitative results from classification analysis controlling for specific actions.

claim: Classification error for sequences in the non-sequential setting was significantly higher (median 0.42, IQR 0.05) compared to the sequence task (median 0.10, IQR 0.14, p<10–12).
source: Moreover, when we performed an equivalent analysis for all sets of consecutive 'Left', 'Left', 'Right' and 'Right', 'Right', Left' triplets found in the choice streams generated when animals made largely independent choices on individual trials (see a detailed explanation in the legend for Figure 1—figure supplement 3), we found a significantly higher classification error (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 3; median cross-validated error 0.42 and IQR 0.05 for the non-sequential setting vs 0.10, IQR 0.14 for the sequence task, p<10–12, Wilcoxon rank-sum test)
evidence: Quantitative comparison with statistical test showing significant difference.

claim: The currently dominant target sequence can be readily decoded from ACC activity during individual actions despite being embedded in indistinguishable choice streams.
source: In such cases, we found that the currently dominant target sequence still could be readily decoded from ACC activity during individual actions such as 'L' despite their being embedded in indistinguishable choice streams (e.g. '…RRLRR…'; Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 3; median cross-validated classification error 0.10, IQR 0.04 and 0.11, 0.05 for side port-centered and center port-centered decoding windows, respectively).
evidence: Quantitative results from classification analysis with matched behavioral streams.

claim: The currently dominant strategy can be decoded from ACC activity when controlling for both immediate past choice and proximity to reward, with median cross-validated error of 0.13 (IQR 0.09) for side port-centered windows.
source: Here too, despite controlling for reward proximity, the currently dominant strategy could readily be decoded (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 3; median cross-validated classification error 0.13, IQR 0.09 and 0.14, 0.11 for side port-centered and center port-centered decoding windows respectively).
evidence: Quantitative results from classification analysis controlling for reward proximity.

claim: At least 76% of all recorded ACC units (787 of 1042 total) displayed significant modulation in at least one of the five analysis windows.
source: At least 76% of all recorded units (787 of 1042 total ACC recorded units, with no separation of potential interneurons) displayed significant modulation in at least one of the five analysis windows – a lower bound given the limitation that the modest size of the exploratory dataset places on the statistical power of these analyses – and a roughly equal fraction of all units displayed modulation in each of the analysis windows (Figure 2f).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of the fraction of modulated units across the recorded population.

claim: The Euclidean distance between the centroids of 'dominant' and 'exploratory' groups was 0.73±0.18 for experimental data versus 0.268±0.077 for shuffled data (p<10–12).
source: Indeed, the Euclidean distance between the centroids of these experimentally observed 'dominant' and 'exploratory' groups differed markedly from that observed when the 'dominant' and 'exploratory' labels were randomly shuffled across the set of all instances of sequence execution (Figure 3d, 0.73±0.18 for experimental data vs 0.268±0.077 for shuffled data, p<10–12, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, n=35 sessions, N=4 animals; 2.6+/-1.9 block changes per session).
evidence: Quantitative comparison with statistical test showing significant separation of clusters.

claim: The mean Euclidean distance between two 'dominant' blocks separated in time was significantly smaller than the mean pairwise distances between a dominant and exploratory block.
source: Moreover, the mean Euclidean distance in the activity state space between two 'dominant' blocks separated in time was significantly smaller than the mean pairwise distances between a dominant and exploratory block, arguing against the possibility that the observed representational transitions in ACC arose from an instability in neural recordings (Figure 3c and d).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of distances between different types of blocks.

claim: Representational changes between distinct exploratory contexts ('LLR' vs 'LLLR' contexts for exploratory 'RRL') showed Euclidean distance of 0.70+/-0.11 versus 0.40+/-0.08 for scrambled labels (p<0.008).
source: Despite the limited statistical power of these smaller exploratory datasets, representational changes between these distinct exploratory contexts were clearly evident both at the single neuron and the population level (Figure 3e, Euclidean distance of 0.70+/-0.11 for two sets of exploratory RRL representations vs 0.40+/-0.08 for a control set with scrambled contextual labels, p<0.008, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, n=5 sessions, 2 animals).
evidence: Quantitative comparison with statistical test showing context-specific representations.

claim: Ensemble states associated with sequence execution during dominant sequence 'tails' did not cluster away from states observed earlier in the 'dominant' context.
source: Ensemble states associated with sequence execution during such dominant sequence 'tails' did not cluster away from states observed earlier in the 'dominant' context, and were equally distant from the exploratory cluster (Figure 3e, Euclidean distance of 0.43+/-0.06 for sequence instances within 'tails' to other dominant sequence instances vs 0.80+/-0.15 for sequence instances within 'tails' to exploratory sequence instances, p<10–6, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, n=17 'tail' examples, N=12 sessions, N=4 rats, 2.1+/-1.1 block changes per session).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of ensemble state distances with statistical comparison.

claim: Ensemble states for 'dominant' but unrewarded 'LLR' sequences did not cluster far from ON-target dominant contexts (Euclidean distance 0.47+/-0.10 for across ON-target vs 0.53+/-0.12 between OFF-target and ON-target, p=0.68).
source: In such cases, ensemble states associated with such 'dominant' but unrewarded 'LLR' sequence instances also did not cluster far away from ones observed earlier in the same session when the dominant 'LLR' strategy matched the rewarded target (Figure 3f, Euclidean distance of 0.47+/-0.10 for across ON-target dominant contexts vs 0.53+/-0.12 between OFF-target and ON-target dominant contexts, p=0.68, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, n=4 sessions, N=2 animals).
evidence: Quantitative comparison showing similarity of ensemble states regardless of reward.

claim: Contextual reorganization of ensemble activity is less pronounced in M2 and SMC compared to ACC, especially in the more caudal SMC.
source: Analysis of the M2 and the SMC ensemble representations associated with individual behavioral sequences over the course of long behavioral sessions revealed that although representational changes could also be observed in those parts of the medial lobe, these changes were significantly less pronounced and affected a smaller fraction of the recorded units, especially in the more caudal SMC (Figure 3g, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Comparative analysis across brain regions showing differential effects.

claim: The model's explanatory power was robust to the precise number of trials in the past used to calculate local sequence prevalence but was diminished if the estimate was shifted to largely comprise future trials.
source: The model's explanatory power was robust to the precise number of trials in the past used to calculate local sequence prevalence but was diminished if the estimate was shifted to largely comprise future trials (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: Analysis showing temporal specificity of the prevalence effect.

claim: The simple behavioral summary statistic of sequence prevalence explained up to 80% of neural activity variance in individual ACC neurons during sequence execution.
source: Strikingly, when we allowed the slope of the linear relationship between the strategy prevalence and the firing rate of individual neurons to vary depending on the global behavioral context, this simple behavioral summary statistic explained up to 80% of neural activity variance in individual ACC neurons during sequence execution (Figure 4b and c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1d; median 28, IQR 42% of activity variance explained by prevalence across all recorded cells in the rostral ACC).
evidence: Quantitative results from linear modeling showing high explanatory power.

claim: The median activity variance explained by prevalence across all recorded cells in the rostral ACC was 28% (IQR 42%).
source: Strikingly, when we allowed the slope of the linear relationship between the strategy prevalence and the firing rate of individual neurons to vary depending on the global behavioral context, this simple behavioral summary statistic explained up to 80% of neural activity variance in individual ACC neurons during sequence execution (Figure 4b and c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1d; median 28, IQR 42% of activity variance explained by prevalence across all recorded cells in the rostral ACC).
evidence: Quantitative summary statistics from linear modeling analysis.

claim: The most substantial modulation by prevalence was observed in the rostral-most portion of ACC thought to be homologous to the primate area 32D.
source: Within the ACC, an encoding potential gradient emerged following a detailed spatial reconstruction of the recorded units, with the most substantial modulation observed in the rostral-most portion thought to be homologous to the primate area 32D (Figure 4b and c).
evidence: Spatial analysis of recording locations showing regional differences in encoding.

claim: The prevalence-based model trained exclusively on 'exploratory' sequence instances explained 0.13 +/- 0.06 of ACC activity variance (n=36 sessions, N=4 animals).
source: The observed model performance in both cases was significantly more robust than what would be expected if most of the observed activity variance during sequence execution arose from the statistics of the associated reward (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a, 0.13 +/- 0.06 of ACC activity variance explained for exploratory sequence instances, n=36 sessions, N=4 animals; Figure 4—figure supplement 2c, 0.35+/–0.23, 0.25+/-0.19 and 0.24+/-0.19 A32D activity variance explained for unrewarded 'LLR' instances dominating early 'LLLR' acquisition in 3 individual animals).
evidence: Quantitative results from modeling analysis on unrewarded trials.

claim: Linear models using execution time or first principal component of movement trajectory could not explain ACC neural activity variance as well as sequence prevalence (0.025+/–0.021 for trajectory, 0.04+/-0.04 for execution time).
source: We first evaluated the performance of an equivalent linear model that used either execution time or the first principal component of movement trajectory as a single parameter; neither model could explain ACC neural activity variance as well as sequence prevalence (Figure 4—figure supplement 3a, 0.025+/–0.021 activity variance explained by movement trajectory, 0.04+/-0.04 by execution time, n=36 sessions, N=4 animals).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of different models showing prevalence has greater explanatory power.

claim: In expanded models including movement parameters, the absolute regression weights were 0.29+/-0.10 for sequence prevalence versus 0.11+/-0.07 for execution time.
source: Consistent with the relatively poor performance of the single movement-related parameter models, the expanded models revealed only a minor contribution from those motor parameters to the overall model's performance (Figure 4—figure supplement 3b, absolute regression weights of 0.29+/-0.10 vs 0.11+/-0.07 for sequence prevalence and execution time; 0.32+/-0.12 and 0.08+/-0.04 for sequence prevalence and movement trajectory; n=36 sessions, N=4 animals).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of regression weights showing prevalence dominates.

claim: The regression weights for sequence prevalence versus movement trajectory were 0.32+/-0.12 and 0.08+/-0.04 respectively (n=36 sessions, N=4 animals).
source: Consistent with the relatively poor performance of the single movement-related parameter models, the expanded models revealed only a minor contribution from those motor parameters to the overall model's performance (Figure 4—figure supplement 3b, absolute regression weights of 0.29+/-0.10 vs 0.11+/-0.07 for sequence prevalence and execution time; 0.32+/-0.12 and 0.08+/-0.04 for sequence prevalence and movement trajectory; n=36 sessions, N=4 animals).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of regression weights in expanded models.

claim: The contribution from 'sequence-specific reward prevalence' was on par with that of 'strategy prevalence', but insufficient on its own to account for the model's explanatory power.
source: Furthermore, while the contribution from the 'sequence-specific reward prevalence' was on par with that of 'strategy prevalence', it was clearly insufficient on its own to account for the model's explanatory power (Figure 4d, regression weights of 0.558+/-0.005 vs 0.122+/-0.003 for sequence prevalence and overall reward prevalence; 0.285+/-0.008 and 0.416+/-0.012 for sequence prevalence and sequence-specific reward prevalence; n=47 sessions, N=9 animals).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of regression weights showing both factors contribute.

claim: Regression weights were 0.558+/-0.005 for sequence prevalence versus 0.122+/-0.003 for overall reward prevalence (n=47 sessions, N=9 animals).
source: Furthermore, while the contribution from the 'sequence-specific reward prevalence' was on par with that of 'strategy prevalence', it was clearly insufficient on its own to account for the model's explanatory power (Figure 4d, regression weights of 0.558+/-0.005 vs 0.122+/-0.003 for sequence prevalence and overall reward prevalence; 0.285+/-0.008 and 0.416+/-0.012 for sequence prevalence and sequence-specific reward prevalence; n=47 sessions, N=9 animals).
evidence: Quantitative results from multiple regression analysis.

claim: Regression weights were 0.285+/-0.008 for sequence prevalence and 0.416+/-0.012 for sequence-specific reward prevalence (n=47 sessions, N=9 animals).
source: Furthermore, while the contribution from the 'sequence-specific reward prevalence' was on par with that of 'strategy prevalence', it was clearly insufficient on its own to account for the model's explanatory power (Figure 4d, regression weights of 0.558+/-0.005 vs 0.122+/-0.003 for sequence prevalence and overall reward prevalence; 0.285+/-0.008 and 0.416+/-0.012 for sequence prevalence and sequence-specific reward prevalence; n=47 sessions, N=9 animals).
evidence: Quantitative results from multiple regression analysis.

claim: Ensembles of ACC neurons containing as few as 10 prevalence-modulated units could explain as much as 60% of sequence prevalence variance.
source: Cross-validated performance of such individually tuned linear decoders scaled steeply with the number of neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a). Moreover, ensembles of ACC neurons containing as few as 10 prevalence-modulated units could explain as much as 60% of sequence prevalence variance.
evidence: Quantitative results from decoding analysis showing ensemble encoding capacity.

claim: The constrained model with fixed weights across windows retained substantial explanatory power (0.23+/-0.02) compared to the best individually tuned models (0.36+/-0.03) (n=36 sessions, N=4 animals).
source: The constrained model retained a large fraction of the overall explanatory power compared to that of the best of five individually tuned decoders (Figure 5b, left panel, variance explained of 0.36+/-0.03 for best of individually tuned models vs 0.23+/-0.02 for the model with weights fixed across the five analysis windows, n=36 sessions, N=4 animals).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of different decoding models.

claim: The ACC is thought to play a critical role in the brain's ability to flexibly deploy strategies effective in complex settings.
source: Medial frontal cortical areas are thought to play a critical role in the brain's ability to flexibly deploy strategies that are effective in complex settings, yet the underlying circuit computations remain unclear.
evidence: Statement in the Abstract referencing established scientific understanding.

claim: The brain's ability to adaptively change behavior is thought to depend on the coordinated action of medial frontal cortical areas.
source: In mammals, the brain's ability to adaptively change behavior is thought to depend on the coordinated action of medial frontal cortical areas that keep track of the information necessary for context-appropriate choices of strategy (Domenech et al., 2020; Donoso et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement citing previous literature on the role of medial frontal cortex.

claim: Functional imaging studies have suggested that ACC is a critical cortical node that translates contextual information into strategy changes.
source: Functional imaging studies in human subjects and non-human primates have suggested that the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), in particular, is a critical cortical node that translates contextual information into strategy changes (Domenech et al., 2020; Donoso et al., 2014; Hayden et al., 2011; Kolling et al., 2012; Sarafyazd and Jazayeri, 2019; Seo et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement citing multiple functional imaging studies.

claim: Previous interpretations of diverse neural responses in ACC have included a direct role in enabling the separation of distinct contexts.
source: Previous interpretations of the diversity of individual neural responses in frontal regions such as the ACC have included a direct role in enabling the separation of distinct contexts (Rigotti et al., 2010), and in tracking the animal's evolving motor state (Musall et al., 2019; Stringer et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement citing previous interpretations from the literature.

claim: ACC has been proposed to track the animal's evolving motor state.
source: Previous interpretations of the diversity of individual neural responses in frontal regions such as the ACC have included a direct role in enabling the separation of distinct contexts (Rigotti et al., 2010), and in tracking the animal's evolving motor state (Musall et al., 2019; Stringer et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement citing previous research on motor state tracking.

claim: Unexpectedly specific ACC responses have been observed in tasks that relaxed experimental control over subjects' behavioral responses.
source: However, unexpectedly specific ACC responses associated with seemingly self-directed strategic choices have also been observed in tasks that relaxed some of the experimental control over subjects' behavioral responses (Schuck et al., 2015; White et al., 2019), raising the possibility that more structured responses in the ACC remain to be discovered.
evidence: Statement citing studies that observed specific ACC responses in less controlled tasks.

claim: One hemodynamic study highlighted the possibility that ACC is specifically engaged during self-guided exploration.
source: One hemodynamic study of the frontal cortical engagement in tasks with less external instruction highlighted the possibility that ACC is specifically engaged during self-guided exploration, with both the self-generation of a specific information-sampling strategy and its evaluation contributing to the observed signal (Walton et al., 2004).
evidence: Statement citing a specific hemodynamic study.

claim: The advantage of choosing one's strategy for sampling information when learning in complex settings has long been appreciated.
source: The advantage of choosing one's strategy for sampling information when learning in complex settings has long been appreciated (Markant and Gureckis, 2014); indeed, the idea that subjects learn more effectively when they self-direct their learning experience is central to many educational philosophies (Boekaerts, 1997; Bruner, 1961).
evidence: Statement citing literature on self-directed learning.

claim: The medial frontal lobe, including SMC and ACC, has been proposed to process information related to self and implement flexible, self-guided actions.
source: As such, it is notable that the medial frontal lobe, including the supplementary motor cortex (SMC) and the ACC, have been proposed to process information related to self, and to implement flexible, self-guided actions (reviewed in Passingham et al., 2010, but see Schüür and Haggard, 2011).
evidence: Statement citing reviews on the role of medial frontal lobe.

claim: The cingulate region features prominently in emerging efforts to experimentally expose task-related information seeking.
source: The cingulate region also features prominently in emerging efforts to experimentally expose task-related information seeking and to uncover its neural underpinnings (Wang and Hayden, 2020; White et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement citing recent research on information seeking.

claim: ACC is thought to play a central role in motivating extended, multi-step behaviors.
source: Indeed, the ACC is thought to play a central role in motivating extended, multi-step behaviors (Holroyd and Yeung, 2012), and our previous work demonstrated the rodent ACC homologue's involvement in unguided discovery of action sequences (Tervo et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement citing literature on ACC's role in multi-step behaviors.

claim: Previous work demonstrated the rodent ACC homologue's involvement in unguided discovery of action sequences.
source: Indeed, the ACC is thought to play a central role in motivating extended, multi-step behaviors (Holroyd and Yeung, 2012), and our previous work demonstrated the rodent ACC homologue's involvement in unguided discovery of action sequences (Tervo et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement citing the authors' previous work.

claim: ACC is known to both multiplex information about reward and individual actions.
source: ACC is known to both multiplex information about reward and individual actions (Hayden and Platt, 2010), as well as track progression to reward over multiple steps of an action sequence (Shidara and Richmond, 2002).
evidence: Statement citing literature on ACC's multiplexing capabilities.

claim: ACC tracks progression to reward over multiple steps of an action sequence.
source: ACC is known to both multiplex information about reward and individual actions (Hayden and Platt, 2010), as well as track progression to reward over multiple steps of an action sequence (Shidara and Richmond, 2002).
evidence: Statement citing literature on ACC's reward tracking.

claim: ACC is thought to guide contextually-appropriate strategy selection.
source: ACC is thought to guide contextually-appropriate strategy selection (reviewed in Heilbronner and Hayden, 2016; Holroyd and Verguts, 2021; Kolling et al., 2016; Monosov et al., 2020; Shenhav et al., 2016)
evidence: Statement citing multiple reviews on ACC function.

claim: Abrupt changes in ACC neuron activity coincident with behavioral transitions to exploration have been reported previously.
source: Indeed, while abrupt changes in the activity of ACC neurons coincident with behavioral transitions to exploration have been reported previously (Durstewitz et al., 2010; Emberly and Seamans Jeremy, 2019; Karlsson et al., 2012; Powell and Redish, 2016)
evidence: Statement citing previous reports of activity changes during exploration.

claim: Studies to define ACC's role in value-based decision-making have emphasized its role in tracking task-relevant information to guide appropriate action.
source: Studies to define the precise role ACC plays in value-based decision-making have emphasized its role in tracking task-relevant information to guide appropriate action, but have otherwise often cast the question in terms of identifying the specific step to which it contributes in the pre-decision computation and comparison of action values (Boorman et al., 2009; Kennerley et al., 2009; Kolling et al., 2012; Luk and Wallis, 2013).
evidence: Statement citing literature on ACC's role in value-based decision-making.

claim: A recent suggestion proposes that ACC encodes post-decision variables related to subjective value inferred from the animal's choices.
source: The resulting lack of a unifying account has prompted a recent suggestion that rather than contributing to pre-decision valuation, ACC encodes post-decision variables related to the subjective value that can be inferred empirically from the animal's choices (Blanchard and Hayden, 2014; Cai and Padoa-Schioppa, 2012).
evidence: Statement citing recent theoretical proposals about ACC function.

claim: 'Network resets' previously observed to accompany transitions to exploration are not mere bookmarks of a behavioral state change, but reflect reorganizations of the ACC network designed to tag action plans with a global context-specific representation.
source: This observation suggests that 'network resets' previously observed to accompany transitions to exploration (Durstewitz et al., 2010; Emberly and Seamans Jeremy, 2019; Karlsson et al., 2012) are not mere bookmarks of a behavioral state change, but rather reflect reorganizations of the ACC network designed to tag action plans with a global context-specific representation.
evidence: Interpretation based on the current findings and previous literature.

claim: The 'dominant'/'exploratory' distinction maps well onto the 'default'/'alternative' dichotomy that has enjoyed prominence in the ACC field.
source: Although 'dominant'/ 'exploratory' distinction maps well onto the 'default'/'alternative' dichotomy that has enjoyed prominence in the ACC field due to its computational appeal and explanatory power in many settings (Blanchard and Hayden, 2014; Boorman et al., 2013; Kolling et al., 2012; Procyk et al., 2000)
evidence: Statement relating current findings to established theoretical frameworks.

claim: ACC's topological centrality within the frontal cortical network and domain-general role in cognition may allow its neural representations to reflect distinct cognitive loads, social settings, or somato-visceral states when appropriate.
source: Indeed, given the ACC's topological centrality within the frontal cortical network and domain-general role in cognition, the content of its neural representations set-up by large-scale re-arrangements of functional networks might come to reflect, when appropriate, distinct cognitive loads (Shenhav et al., 2016), social settings (Tomlin et al., 2006) or somato-visceral states (Caracheo et al., 2018; Seamans and Floresco, 2022).
evidence: Speculative statement citing literature on various ACC functions.

claim: ACC's well-documented role in exploration suggests that keeping track of strategy prevalence may be used to prioritize exploring strategies evaluated less frequently in the recent past.
source: Given ACC's well-documented role in exploration (Blanchard and Hayden, 2014; Fouragnan et al., 2019; Hayden et al., 2011; Kolling et al., 2012; Quilodran et al., 2008; Tervo et al., 2021), one possibility is that keeping track of strategy prevalence may be used to prioritize exploring strategies evaluated less frequently in the recent past (see Wiering and Schmidhuber, 1998 for one implementation of such frequency-based exploration).
evidence: Speculative interpretation citing literature on exploration.

claim: An intriguing possibility is that keeping track of different actions and their frequency might be an effective way of estimating agency through statistical learning.
source: Indeed, an intriguing possibility is that in complex settings, keeping track of different actions taken and the frequency with which one has performed them might be an effective way of estimating agency – an understanding of which actions bring about the ability to promote or prevent the occurrence of events in the environment – through statistical learning.
evidence: Speculative interpretation proposing a novel computational role.

claim: Statistical learning is thought to be central to many aspects of perceptual cognition and motor control.
source: Statistical learning is thought to be central to many aspects of perceptual cognition and motor control; in the causal domain, it provides a complement to associative learning in permitting the agent to make inferences about the world without being enslaved to temporal contiguity or specific action-outcome contingencies.
evidence: Statement about established role of statistical learning.

claim: One influential view posits that behind the efficiency of statistical learning is the process of probabilistic inference that entertains multiple candidate models coupled with explicit hypothesis testing.
source: However, one influential view posits that behind the efficiency, with which animals pick up on statistical regularities from sparse data in complex, often only partially observable environments, is the process of probabilistic inference that entertains multiple candidate models of the underlying statistical regularities coupled with explicit hypothesis testing designed to evaluate those models (Tenenbaum et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement citing an influential theoretical framework.

claim: ACC's central role in establishing one's agency reconciles the finding of robust prevalence encoding with causal evidence linking it to decisions about evaluating alternative action plans.
source: We posit that ACC's central role in establishing one's agency is what reconciles our finding of its robust prevalence encoding and the causal evidence (Tervo et al., 2020) linking it to the ongoing decision of whether or not to evaluate alternative action plans (and more generally to curiosity Wang and Hayden, 2020, information seeking White et al., 2019 and hypothesis testing Elliott and Dolan, 1998).
evidence: Interpretive statement integrating current findings with previous causal evidence.

claim: The interpretation that ACC plays a key role in evaluating agency is a refinement of the hypothesis that it processes information related to self and implements self-generated actions.
source: We note that the interpretation that ACC – and likely the medial frontal network into which it is embedded – plays a key role in evaluating the extent to which one has agency in the environment is a refinement of the broader hypothesis that it processes information related to self and implements self-generated actions that not only accommodates the existing experimental observations but is also more falsifiable.
evidence: Interpretive statement proposing a refined theoretical framework.

claim: A major critique of the 'self-generated actions' view of the medial frontal lobe is that the distinction between self-generated and externally triggered actions is empirically intractable.
source: Indeed, a major critique of the 'self-generated actions' view of the medial frontal lobe is that the distinction between self-generated and externally triggered actions is empirically intractable, thus making this view of the medial frontal lobe unfalsifiable (Schüür and Haggard, 2011).
evidence: Statement citing a critique from the literature.

claim: It is conceivable to develop experimental designs that manipulate reward statistics to induce miscalculations of agency such as superstitions and learned helplessness.
source: In contrast, it is conceivable to develop experimental designs that manipulate the reward statistics to induce miscalculations of agency: superstitions – a perception of control over the environment in the absence of a causal link between the agents' actions and the outcome, and learned helplessness – an incorrect perception of a lack of control and a cessation of action.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential future experiments.

claim: Each tetrode was constructed by twisting and fusing together four insulated 13 μm wires.
source: Each tetrode was constructed by twisting and fusing together four insulated 13 μm wires (stablohm 800 A, California Fine Wire).
evidence: Direct statement in Methods describing electrode construction.

claim: Each tetrode tip was gold-plated to reduce impedance to 200–300 kΩ at 1 kHz.
